title: How ZIP Compression (DEFLATE) Works
summary: ZIP files compress data using the DEFLATE algorithm, which pairs LZ77 duplicate string matching with Huffman frequency bit encoding.

body.definition: A standardized lossless data compression algorithm combining LZ77 dictionary substitution with dynamic Huffman entropy coding.

body.text: Created by Phil Katz in 1989 for PKZIP, the format operates in two sequential stages: First, LZ77 scans data for repeated strings within a sliding 32 KB window, replacing duplicates with `(distance, length)` back-pointers. Second, Huffman coding replaces frequent symbols with shorter bit patterns.
ZIP File Structure

items: Local File Headers: Metadata and compressed payload for each individual file stored sequentially.
Central Directory: Placed at the end of the ZIP archive, listing all files and offset pointers for instant file seeking without full extraction.
End of Central Directory (EOCD): The final record that archive readers read first to locate the central directory table.

body.text: Android APKs, Java JARs, and Microsoft Office DOCX/XLSX files are internally standard ZIP archives with renamed file extensions.

title: Lossless vs Lossy Data Compression
summary: Lossless compression reconstructs data perfectly bit-for-bit, while lossy compression discards imperceptible human perceptual data to achieve massive size reductions.

body.definition: A data encoding method that achieves high compression ratios by permanently discarding inexact, redundant, or psychovisually unnoticeable data.

body.text: Executables, source code, text documents, and databases require lossless compression (ZIP, GZIP, PNG, FLAC) because a single altered bit corrupts the entire program. Media streaming (JPEG, MP3, MP4, WebP) uses lossy compression, exploiting human eye and ear limitations to shrink files by 80% to 95%.
Comparison Summary

rows.label: Decompressed Quality
values: Slightly degraded / loss of high frequencies

rows.label: Primary Use Cases
values: Executables, text, code, medical scans, FLAC
Streaming video, web photos, music streaming

body.text: Generation loss occurs when a lossy file is repeatedly decompressed, edited, and re-saved in lossy formats, compounding visual artifacts.

title: Shannon Entropy & Theoretical Compression Limits
summary: Shannon's Source Coding Theorem establishes the absolute mathematical lower bound of bits required to encode information without data loss.

body.definition: A mathematical metric introduced by Claude Shannon quantifying the average information content, uncertainty, and surprise conveyed by a data source.

body.text: The formula `H(X) = -sum(P(x) * log2(P(x)))` calculates the minimum theoretical bit-length needed per symbol. If data is completely random (like an encrypted file or already compressed archive), entropy equals 8 bits per byte and no lossless algorithm in existence can compress it further.
Key Implications

items: Pigeonhole Principle: No lossless compression algorithm can compress all possible inputs; if some files shrink, others must mathematically expand.
Compression as Predictability: High compression ratios are only achievable on highly predictable data with low information entropy.
Asymmetric Numeral Systems (ANS): Modern entropy encoders (used in Zstandard) achieve Shannon-limit compression with extreme throughput.

body.text: Attempting to compress an encrypted file (like a VeraCrypt volume or HTTPS stream) will produce zero compression because cryptographic ciphers output high-entropy pseudo-random bytes.

title: Huffman Coding & Prefix Codes
summary: Huffman coding builds a binary frequency tree that assigns shorter variable-length bit codes to frequent characters and longer bit codes to rare ones.

body.definition: A binary tree constructed from character frequency weights to generate optimal prefix-free variable-length binary codes.

body.text: Standard ASCII text uses 8 fixed bits for every single character. In English text, the letter 'E' appears thousands of times while 'Z' appears rarely. Huffman coding assigns a short 2-bit code (e.g. `01`) to 'E' and a longer 9-bit code to 'Z', reducing average storage requirements by 30% to 50%.
Prefix-Free Property

items: No code in a Huffman dictionary is a prefix of any other code.
Because of prefix-freedom, the decoder can stream and parse compressed bits sequentially without needing any explicit delimiter or space characters.
Canonical Huffman codes sort symbols lexicographically, allowing tree tables to be transmitted in a fraction of the header size.

body.text: Huffman coding is the foundational entropy-stage compressor inside JPEG images, MP3 audio, and ZIP archives.

title: Run-Length Encoding (RLE)
summary: Run-Length Encoding compresses consecutive identical data values into a single value count and byte pair, excelling on simple graphics and bitmaps.

body.definition: A straightforward lossless compression algorithm that replaces consecutive sequences ('runs') of repeated data items with a single data value and count.

body.text: If uncompressed image data contains `WWWWWWWWWWWWBWWWWWWWWWWWW` (12 Whites, 1 Black, 12 Whites = 25 bytes), RLE encodes it as `12W1B12W` (6 bytes), achieving a 76% size reduction. However, on noisy or photographic data with no repeated bytes, RLE expands file size.
Practical Applications

items: Fax Machines (CCITT Group 3/4): Black-and-white scanned lines contain long runs of pure white space compressed via 1D/2D RLE.
Bitmap Icons & BMP: 8-bit paletted icons with flat color fields.
JPEG DC Coefficients: Used as an intermediate step after Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) quantization generates long runs of trailing zeroes.

body.text: RLE requires minimal CPU overhead, making it ideal for low-power embedded microcontrollers and vintage game consoles.

title: Archive Formats: ZIP vs RAR vs 7z
summary: ZIP prioritizes universal compatibility, RAR offers solid archives with recovery records, and 7z achieves maximum compression ratios via LZMA/LZMA2.

body.definition: A compression mode that treats all files in an archive as a single continuous continuous data stream, allowing dictionary matches across different files.

body.text: Standard ZIP compresses each file individually, enabling instant extraction of a single file but missing redundancies across multiple files. 7z and RAR use solid compression, finding identical patterns across thousands of separate files to achieve dramatically smaller archives.
Format Comparison
RAR's Reed-Solomon Recovery Records allow damaged archives with bad disk sectors to be repaired and extracted without corruption.

title: Tarballs (.tar.gz & .tar.zst)
summary: A tarball bundles thousands of files and Unix permissions into a single stream, which is then passed to a stream compressor like GZIP, XZ, or Zstandard.

body.definition: A standard Unix archive format created in 1979 that concatenates files, directories, POSIX ownership, and permission metadata into a single sequential byte stream.

body.text: Following the Unix philosophy ('do one thing and do it well'), `tar` does not perform any compression on its own; it merely bundles directory trees into a single `.tar` archive. That `.tar` stream is then piped into a dedicated compression utility like Gzip (`.tar.gz`), XZ (`.tar.xz`), or Zstandard (`.tar.zst`).
Common Tarball Flags

items: `tar -czvf archive.tar.gz /path`: Creates (`c`) a Gzipped (`z`) verbose (`v`) archive file (`f`).
`tar -xzvf archive.tar.gz`: Extracts (`x`) an existing Gzipped tarball.
`tar --zstd -cvf archive.tar.zst /path`: Creates a modern Zstandard-compressed archive with ultra-fast multi-threaded decompression.

body.text: Arch Linux packages and modern Linux kernels use Zstandard (`.tar.zst`) because it decompresses at over 3 GB/s per core.
